_about: Each entry puts one known bug back into internal/web and the suite must fail. The set is weighted toward the security decisions rather than the plumbing: a mutant that survives on the CSRF layer or the certificate store means the test suite does not actually pin the control it claims to. Run: python3 scripts/mutate.py scripts/mutations/web.json

the CSRF comparison leaks timing on a secret. The mutant adds `got == want ||` in front of the constant-time compare. The two
expressions return the same bool for every possible pair of inputs, so no test can
distinguish them: the only difference is how long the comparison takes, and timing
is not an observable a unit test in this package has.

Marking it equivalent is a claim, so it is checkable: delete the `got == want ||`
prefix and every test in internal/web still passes -- in particular
TestAPostWithoutACSRFTokenIsRefusedAndDoesNothing,
TestAPostWithTheSessionsTokenIsAccepted and
TestAnotherSessionsCSRFTokenIsNotAccepted, which together pin that a correct token
is accepted, a missing one is refused, and another session's token is refused. All
three go through this comparison, so they pin that it exists and is reached; none of
them can pin that it is constant-time.

What the mutant is really guarding against -- someone swapping the constant-time
compare for a plain == -- is therefore a review property, not a test property.
the login form can be framed by a hostile page
a dynamic page is cacheable, so who is locked out stays readable after logout
the panic text reaches the client, mapping the binary for anybody on the LAN
a panic is turned into a 500 and never logged, so nobody knows it happened
a JSON client following a redirect gets an HTML login page where it expected a status code
a refused CSRF check leaves no trace
the transport accepts anything a client offers
a content-addressed asset is re-fetched on every page view
an unknown hash falls back to the literal name, so the immutable header can pin a stale file forever
the auth gate lets an anonymous request through

mutants.note: in-flight requests are cut off instead of drained
the asset URL hashes the filename, so a content change keeps the same URL and the immutable header pins the old bytes
Serve stops terminating TLS, so a daemon configured `auto` answers plain HTTP on a port it logs as https:// and the Secure cookie can never be set
a broken asset bundle is swallowed, so every /static/ request 404s and the operator gets the unstyled page with nothing in the log
the disabled-transport warning ignores Options.Warn and goes to stdout, the stream an operator redirects away

the resolved asset map is dropped on the floor, so New succeeds and every /static/ request 404s: the operator gets the unstyled page that embedding the assets exists to prevent, with nothing in the log. Re-pointed twice now: it used to match a line in New's composite literal, and gofmt re-spaces those when any field is added, so an unrelated Options field retired the mutant while the suite stayed green. It targets a statement now, whose spacing does not depend on its neighbours.
the bind signal is never sent, so every caller of WaitReady blocks until its own deadline -- the dead field's contract, broken in the other direction
the waiter is released but never told what happened, so a failed bind reports success and the caller reads an empty Addr() with no error to explain it
a Server assembled as a struct literal gets a nil channel, and closing it panics in Serve -- the zero-value rule this package's own tests depend on
a caller that gave up is told the server is ready, so a daemon that never bound looks healthy to the thing supervising it

the enforcement loop dropped from the daemon's runners: the admin UI is served, the dashboard looks healthy, and nobody is ever locked out. This is the exact regression the branch's own 'not wired into this build' notice existed to catch, and a notice is not a test. Widened to cover the assembly when serveEngine extracted the field assignments -- deleting `engine.Run,` alone left the variable unused, so the mutant had become a build failure rather than a bug.

the guard counts constructed backends instead of usable ones -- the exact defect a review caught. Names() lists what the registry could build, and a constructor only fails on a nil runner or an unknown id, so this fires on a typo in lockBackends and stays silent on a machine where loginctl exists and exits 1. The daemon then announces that enforcement is running, serves the admin UI, and can lock nobody. Written as the regression rather than as a generic weakening, so the battery keeps guarding the specific mistake

the audit pre-flight removed: the writer opens lazily, so an unwritable trail surfaces as the first dropped event hours later instead of as a startup failure the operator who can fix it is standing in front of

the startup line sent nowhere. This is the guard whose absence broke CI and not the author's desktop: it is the only stdout write that does not depend on a lock backend answering the probe, so TestTheTLSSWarningIsNotOnStdout's premise -- that stdout carries something before the warning -- was quietly a fact about the machine. A daemon whose log records only exceptions does not say it came up, and does not say which config it opened, which is the one mistake that reads as success

the availability report is printed but never counted, so usable stays 0 and a machine that can lock somebody is refused at startup. This is the direction the guard could be 'fixed' in to look safe: refusing always passes every refusal test, so the control -- a usable backend must start -- is what this mutant needs, and TestServeStartsWhenOneBackendIsUsable is what kills it
a server built without its configuration source renders a dashboard from a nil config, so the missing wiring advertises an empty household forever instead of refusing
a source that answers (nil, nil) is handed to the view builder, which reads it as 'no accounts are managed'
the accounts page renders an empty table when it never looked at the password file
the accounts page is rendered from an empty union, so the unmanaged count and the table both describe a machine nobody logged into
the page is streamed instead of buffered, so a template that fails halfway leaves half a document on the wire behind a 200 and a browser renders half a table as a whole one
the page becomes cacheable, so a parent can be shown a stale answer about whether their child is locked out -- and a shared proxy can hold it
the stylesheet is linked by its plain name, so it is served under the page's no-store or not at all, and a fix to app.css does not appear on a parent's phone until the browser feels like revalidating
a nil session source becomes an empty session list, which the page renders as 'nobody has a desktop session' -- a claim about the machine the daemon never established

mutants.old: s.logf("web: %s session list unavailable: %v", requestID(r), err)
mutants.note: the session column failing is silent, so 'locked out' on the dashboard reads as 'the screen is locked right now' with nothing saying the column that means that is missing

the pages are rendered with text/template, so an account name -- the one field on the page a child with a shell on the box can plausibly control -- is written into the document as markup instead of as a name

the rotation is noticed and nothing is revoked: the stolen session keeps resolving for its full sliding window and the log line still claims the sessions ended. This is the whole of #37 -- the sentence 'every existing admin session ends' was false for exactly this reason.

the first read is treated as a rotation, so every daemon restart ends every session -- an operator logged out by a config reload, with a log line claiming the credential changed when nobody rotated anything.

mutants.old: s.logf("web: admin credential could not be re-read: %v", err)
mutants.new:
s.Sessions.RevokeAll()
			s.logf("web: admin credential could not be re-read: %v", err)
mutants.note: a transient config read error becomes a mass logout. The file is replaced rather than truncated, so a read can fail because the watcher arrived between the unlink and the rename -- an availability fault dressed up as a security event.

a handed Authenticator outranks the configuration. That is the shape `plock serve` had: srv.Auth captured the verifier at startup, so the daemon kept accepting the pre-rotation password while the watcher logged that it had ended sessions. The config is the only source of truth for the credential, so it wins.

the watcher starts with no configuration source, so a server that has nothing to read complains on every tick forever -- and the one line that means a rotation took effect is buried in noise the operator learns to ignore.

the account source is wired but answers nothing, so /users 503s on the real daemon while every test that stubs the seam stays green. The call is kept so the import stays used and the mutant compiles. Re-pointed onto the Listing signature the seam now carries

mutants.note: the session listing is wired but returns nothing, so the dashboard says nobody is logged in on a machine with children at desks. This is the fail-open shape of the seam: a missing seam makes the pages refuse loudly, a hollow one reports a quiet house. `srv.Lockables != nil` cannot see it, which is exactly how the original wiring test passed while the body did nothing.

the listing is handed a fresh background context instead of the serve context, so a shutdown has no way to cancel a session query that is already in flight and the drain waits on work it cannot interrupt.

serve resolving the location and never saying so: the operator's only startup signal that an account is going unenforced is gone, and the audit line is one line in a file nobody tails. TestServeSaysWhenItWillNotLockItsOwnSession.

serve telling the enforcement loop it is inside a login session and telling the dashboard nothing. The page then reports that account as locked out while the engine declines to lock it -- the fail-open reading of a row, on the one surface the parent actually reads. TestServeHandsTheDashboardTheSameLocationItHandsTheEngine.

the constructor dropping the location, so every assembled Server behaves as a system unit regardless of what its caller knows. A fixture that sets Server.Self by hand stays green while the documented constructor cannot deliver it. TestServeHandsTheDashboardTheSameLocationItHandsTheEngine.

the trim becomes a no-op, so a reason of one space passes the blank check and is stored and audited as nothing -- and the stored value stops matching what the operator wrote. TrimLeft(raw, "") rather than dropping the call: an unused import is a build failure the battery prints as a catch.

the length bound disappears, so a client can store a reason of any size in the one file the daemon must read every tick and in every audit line after it. The writer is an authenticated admin, so this is durability and legibility, not an attack surface -- which is exactly why the refusal has to name the number.

mutants.new: if cc, ok := view.(csrfCarrier); ok && false {
mutants.note: render stops handing the token to page bodies, so every form a page renders is refused by the CSRF gate on submit -- the #59 dead-button defect, arriving again by a different route. `ok && false` rather than an empty body: cc and ok would then be declared and unused, which is a build failure, not a catch.

the value instead of the pointer: setCSRF has a pointer receiver, so a value does not satisfy csrfCarrier and the dashboard renders its forms with no token while every other page still works. This is the trap the comment above the call warns about, pinned so it cannot come back quietly.

mutants.old: return audit.Tail{}, errors.New("no audit trail is wired")
mutants.note: the unwired seam reporting an empty trail instead of refusing. This is the whole reason the seam exists as an interface with a named refusal: a zero Tail and a nil error is indistinguishable from a machine that has recorded nothing, so the page renders 'the trail is empty' about a build that cannot look at all. The dashboard's session seam has the same mutant for the same reason. TestAnUnwiredTrailNeverClaimsTheTrailIsEmpty

any read error becoming a page error, so a trail that is one unreadable generation short stops showing the records that were read. The reader's contract is to return both -- records and the reason the page is short -- and treating the reason as fatal throws away the half an operator needs. TestAPartialTrailShowsWhatWasReadAndSaysItIsIncomplete

a short page presented as a complete one to anything that is not a browser. The sentence on the page is for the parent; the header is for the script, and a monitoring check that parses the page cannot tell 3 of 200 from 200 of 200. Same signal the dashboard sets for a failed session read. TestAPartialTrailShowsWhatWasReadAndSaysItIsIncomplete

the filter inverted, which is the shape that survives a careless review because the page still shows a plausible table with plausible names. A substring match is the other way this breaks -- 'cat' merging with 'catie' on the one page whose job is saying who was held -- but that needs a strings import the file does not have, so it cannot be expressed as a single-site mutation; the exact-match test is what pins it. TestTheAuditFilterMatchesAccountsExactly

Scanned counts the probe record instead of the window. The caption then tells the operator the filter only saw the most recent 201 -- a number the page never showed -- and the row count and the searched count stop describing the same read. Killed by the caption assertion in TestARecordBehindTheWindowSaysTheReadStoppedEarly.

a machine with no trail file yet told its operator the trail is empty. Those are two different facts and only one of them means the writer is working: 'no trail file exists' is what a fresh install should say, and 'the trail is empty' is what a misconfigured writer says, which is the sentence that should make a parent go and check permissions. TestAMissingTrailFileSaysNothingHasBeenRecorded

the audit page registered without the session gate. It is the page that names which accounts were locked out and when, and it is the only route in the table whose data comes from a file rather than from the request, so an unauthenticated read of it is a read of the machine's history. TestTheContentPagesRequireASession

the window quietly shrunk, which is the defect that cannot be seen from the page: 20 events is about four minutes of a busy daemon, and every sentence on the page stays true while the answer to 'when was she last held' walks out of range. The test asserts the literal 200 rather than the constant, which is why this mutant dies at all. TestTheAuditPageListsEventsNewestFirst

the page reading the default path while the daemon writes the one --audit-path named. Nothing about this is nil, so the nil check in TestServeWiresEverySeamThePagesRead passes; the reader opens a file nobody writes, finds nothing, and the page says the trail is empty about a trail that is full. The same shape as the config source, arriving through a path constant. TestTheServedAuditTrailIsTheFileTheOperatorNamed

serve assembling the page's seam out of a reader that is not there, so GET /audit answers 503 on the real daemon while every page test stays green because each one wires its own seam by hand. This is the failure the whole serve_seams_test.go file exists for. TestServeWiresEverySeamThePagesRead

Always claim the read stopped early. A trail that ends at the window then sends the operator to search older events that do not exist, which is the over-claim #91 is about, arrived at by removing the test instead of weakening it. Killed by TestATrailOfExactlyTheWindowIsExhaustedNotTruncated.

Never claim the read stopped early. With a record genuinely behind the window the page says the trail holds nothing older, and an operator concludes an account was never held when the older events are one record away. Killed by TestARecordBehindTheWindowSaysTheReadStoppedEarly.

Drop the probe: ask the reader for exactly the window. Tail returns min(n, total) with a nil error, so a trail of exactly 200 and a trail of 500 become the same result again and the page is back to guessing at the boundary. Killed by the request assertion in TestTheAuditPageListsEventsNewestFirst, which pins 201 as a literal so it cannot drift with the constant.

Cut the probe off the wrong end: drop the newest event and keep the record that only exists as evidence. The page still shows 200 rows and still says 200 of 200, so nothing about the shape changes except that the first row an operator reads is gone. Killed by the newest-record assertion in TestARecordBehindTheWindowSaysTheReadStoppedEarly.

serve assembles the enforcement loop and never hands it the login session it is running inside. The loop then runs at the zero value, the self-session rule never fires, and the daemon locks the screen it is running behind -- so it can no longer be stopped -- while the dashboard still reports that account as declined. Issue #72: this line had no test and no mutant, and deleting it left the whole suite green, because the loop's own tests set the field by hand. TestServeHandsTheDashboardTheSameLocationItHandsTheEngine.

the engine keeps enforce.New's default logger instead of the sink serve was given. Nothing breaks loudly: the daemon runs, and the two lines an operator needs when enforcement quietly stopped -- a tick that fell behind, a config that would not reload -- go to the process's stderr instead of the configured sink, so a redirect misses them. TestServeHandsTheEngineItsLogSink.

an absent profile stops being recognised, so it lands in the default branch and answers 503 'the profile could not be deleted' -- retryable-looking, when retrying can never help. TestDeletingAProfileThatDoesNotExistIsNotFound.

mutants.old: s.pageRefuse(w, r, http.StatusNotFound, "there is no profile with that id")
mutants.note: the 404 goes back to echoing the error, which puts request-supplied text (the profile id comes from the URL) into the response body. This is the shape that let a hostile id state a falsehood about enforcement. TestAHostileProfileIDCannotChooseWhichRefusalFires.

mutants.old: s.mutateRefused(w, r, "the profile could not be deleted", err)
mutants.note: the finding the reviewer measured: a seam failure (read-only mount, full disk, corrupt config) reported as 'no such profile' with the raw error echoed. TestASeamFailureIsNotReportedAsAMissingProfile.

Caught at the layer that owns the contract by TestTheTwoDeletionRefusalsCarryTheirSentinels; the web-side consequence is pinned by W105 and W107, which mutate the branches themselves.

same shape on the other refusal: the wording is unchanged, the identity is gone. TestTheTwoDeletionRefusalsCarryTheirSentinels, plus TestAMissingProfileNamesTheIDItCouldNotFind for the id the CLI prints.
